Chapter One: The What and Why of Continu.point: 产品决策天天在做，客户输入也必须以同样的频率进入决策
Chapter One: The What and Why of Continu.core: Product teams make decisions every day. Our goal with continuous discovery is to infuse those daily decisions with as much customer input as possible.
Chapter One: The What and Why of Continu.case: Discovery happened once a year in an annual budgeting process, where projects with fixed timelines were assigned to specific engineering teams. A project manager managed the work, budget, and schedule. Sometimes a product manager translated business needs to product requirements, but not always. There were (and still are) many challenges with this way of working. Software development is unpredictable. Projects were often delivered late and over budget. Business needs often trumped customer needs. Teams learned after the product shipped that customers weren’t excited about what they built.
Chapter One: The What and Why of Continu.explain: 年度预算制下发现一年只发生一次，团队在发布后才发现客户并不兴奋，说明低频客户输入让大量日常决策脱离客户，造成浪费。

Chapter Two: A Common Framework for Cont.point: 追求业务结果时，要用以客户为中心的方式框定问题
Chapter Two: A Common Framework for Cont.core: If product trios tasked with delivering a desired outcome want to pursue business value by creating customer value, they’ll need to work to frame the problem in a customer-centric way.
Chapter Two: A Common Framework for Cont.case: For example, in the Wells Fargo story, their leadership, whether implicitly or explicitly, had framed the problem as “grow customer accounts at all costs.” This framing opened the door to cheating. If, on the other hand, Wells Fargo had framed the problem as “create customers who want to open more accounts,” bankers would have been less likely to cheat.
Chapter Two: A Common Framework for Cont.explain: 富国银行把问题框定为“不惜代价增长账户”，导致员工私自开户；若框定为“让客户愿意多开户”，就会引导团队创造客户价值而非造假。

Chapter Three: Focusing on Outcomes Over.point: 三人组更适合负责自己可控的产品结果，而非滞后的业务结果
Chapter Three: Focusing on Outcomes Over.core: As a general rule, product trios will make more progress on a product outcome rather than a business outcome. Remember, product outcomes measure how well the product moves the business forward.
Chapter Three: Focusing on Outcomes Over.case: First, not all tails.com customers understood the value of tailor-made dog food, and, second, some dogs simply didn’t like the food. Sonja’s team realized that they could prevent churn, and thus increase retention, if they focused on increasing the perceived value of tailor-made dog food and if they increased the number of dogs that liked the food.
Chapter Three: Focusing on Outcomes Over.explain: tails.com 团队被分配提升留存这一业务结果，但留存是滞后指标，难以快速实验；他们转而聚焦提升定制狗粮的感知价值、让更多狗爱吃，即产品结果，从而推动留存。

Chapter Four: Visualizing What You Know.point: 先各自画体验地图再合并，避免群体思维，汇集不同视角
Chapter Four: Visualizing What You Know.core: To prevent groupthink, it’s critical that each member of the trio start by developing their own perspective before the trio works together to develop a shared perspective.
Chapter Four: Visualizing What You Know.case: The product manager had the best grasp of the “known” challenges—the customer complaints that made their way to their call center and through support tickets. The designer missed a few steps in the process but did a great job of capturing the confusion and insecurity that the customer might be feeling in the process. Because he was new to the company, he was able to view the application process from an outsider’s perspective. The engineer’s map accurately captured the process and added detail about how one step informed another step.
Chapter Four: Visualizing What You Know.explain: 产品经理、设计师、工程师各自画申请流程地图：产品经理熟悉投诉，设计师捕捉到客户的不安，新人工程师以局外人视角补全流程细节。三张图合并后，分歧点成为访谈要验证的地方。

Chapter Five: Continuous Interviewing.point: 不要直接问客户怎么做，而要让他们讲述具体的最近一次经历
Chapter Five: Continuous Interviewing.core: Since we can’t ask our customers direct questions about their behavior, the best way to learn about their needs, pain points, and desires is to ask them to share specific stories about their experience.
Chapter Five: Continuous Interviewing.case: During a workshop, I asked a woman what factors she considered when buying a new pair of jeans. She didn’t hesitate to answer. She said, “Fit is my number-one factor.” I then asked her to tell me about the last time she bought a pair of jeans. She said, “I bought them on Amazon.” I asked, “How did you know they would fit?” She replied, “I didn’t, but they were a brand I liked, and they were on sale.”
Chapter Five: Continuous Interviewing.explain: 女士被问买牛仔裤看重什么时答“合身最重要”，但讲上次购买经历时却说没试就因品牌和打折在亚马逊下单——具体故事暴露了真实行为与自我描述的矛盾。

Chapter Six: Mapping the Opportunity Spa.point: 绘制机会空间，是给结构不良的问题赋予结构的方法
Chapter Six: Mapping the Opportunity Spa.core: Mapping the opportunity space is how we give structure to the ill-structured problem of reaching our desired outcome.
Chapter Six: Mapping the Opportunity Spa.case: Their marketplace had little Istraha inventory, and the team needed to figure out how to entice hosts to share their properties and how to get guests to consider their platform as the place to book. Guijou’s team turned to their continuous discovery habits to guide them. They started interviewing Istraha hosts and guests. They uncovered countless opportunities on both sides of the marketplace. Rather than getting overwhelmed, they started mapping out the needs of each group on respective opportunity solution trees.
Chapter Six: Mapping the Opportunity Spa.explain: Seera 团队面对度假屋市场供需两端的模糊难题，没有陷入海量访谈发现，而是把房东与房客的需求分别画成机会解决方案树，用树结构把无从下手的问题拆成可逐层处理的分支。

Chapter Six: Mapping the Opportunity Spa.point: 树结构能把大而难的问题拆成一系列更易解决的小问题
Chapter Six: Mapping the Opportunity Spa.explain: “这部剧好看吗”这类大问题难以直接下手，而“那个演员是谁”更易解决；树结构让团队看清难易机会的层级关系，从而逐步拆解、逐个攻克。
Chapter Six: Mapping the Opportunity Spa.core: When we learn to think in the structure of trees, it helps us deconstruct large, intractable problems into a series of smaller, more solvable problems.
Chapter Six: Mapping the Opportunity Spa.case: “Is this show any good?” feels like a big, hard problem. How do we evaluate “good” for each individual viewer? “Who is that actor?” feels much easier. Should we always prioritize easy over hard? If so, when do we ever get to the hard problems that have the potential to differentiate us from our competitors and really drive our outcomes?

Chapter Seven: Prioritizing Opportunitie.point: 选择目标机会是可逆的双向门决策，应快速决定而非等待完美数据
Chapter Seven: Prioritizing Opportunitie.core: When we assess and prioritize the opportunity space, even though these are some of the most strategic decisions we make as a product trio, we are still making two-way door decisions.
Chapter Seven: Prioritizing Opportunitie.case: He describes a Level 1 decision as one that is hard to reverse, whereas a Level 2 decision is one that is easy to reverse. Bezos argues that we should be slow and cautious when making Level 1 decisions, but that we should move fast and not wait for perfect data when making Level 2 decisions.
Chapter Seven: Prioritizing Opportunitie.explain: 贝索斯把决策分为难逆转的Level 1和易逆转的Level 2，主张后者应快速行动、不必等完美数据。机会优先排序正属此类可逆决策，故应快速决定。

Chapter Eight: Supercharged Ideation.point: 个人独立构思胜过集体头脑风暴，应先个人发散再交流
Chapter Eight: Supercharged Ideation.core: So, if we stick to what the research tells us, individuals generating ideas on their own do outperform brainstorming groups.
Chapter Eight: Supercharged Ideation.case: For decades researchers ran studies in which they compared the creative output of brainstorming groups against the creative output of the same number of individuals generating ideas alone. Study after study found that the individuals generating ideas alone outperformed the brainstorming groups. Individuals generated more ideas, more diverse ideas, and more original ideas.
Chapter Eight: Supercharged Ideation.explain: 数十年对照研究反复发现，同样人数下，独立构思者比头脑风暴小组产出更多、更多样、更原创的想法，直接证明集体讨论会抑制创意，应先各自发散。

Chapter Nine: Identifying Hidden Assumpt.point: 团队容易爱上自己的想法而过度自信，必须主动挖掘隐藏假设
Chapter Nine: Identifying Hidden Assumpt.core: We tend to seek out why our ideas will work and forget to explore why they might not work. As a result, we are often overconfident about the success of our ideas.
Chapter Nine: Identifying Hidden Assumpt.case: The developer built a building consisting primarily of one- and two-bedroom units. Both the city council and the developer thought this was how they could maximize impact and help the most families. Unfortunately, most of the displaced families were families of four or more. One- or two-bedroom condos wouldn’t work for them. The city spent millions of dollars building the wrong product for the outcome they wanted.
Chapter Nine: Identifying Hidden Assumpt.explain: 市议会和开发商都以为建一居、两居室能帮到最多家庭，却没检验“受益家庭是四口以上”这一隐藏假设，结果花数百万建错产品，正说明过度自信会漏掉关键假设。

Chapter Ten: Testing Assumptions, Not Id.point: 测试前要定好具体的评估标准，团队才能一致解读结果
Chapter Ten: Testing Assumptions, Not Id.core: To avoid this situation, we want to get specific with our evaluation criteria. Instead of saying, “Some people choose sports,” we want to say, “At least 3 out of 10 people choose sports.”
Chapter Ten: Testing Assumptions, Not Id.case: The problem with “some” is that your product manager might define “some” as 5 out of 10, and your designer might define “some” as 20 out of 100. If you run your simulation with 10 people, and 6 people choose sports, your product manager is going to think your assumption is now more known, and your designer is still going to be skeptical.
Chapter Ten: Testing Assumptions, Not Id.explain: 案例中“一些”被产品经理理解为5/10、设计师理解为20/100，10人测试6人选择时两人结论相反；说明模糊标准导致解读分歧，具体数字才能对齐团队。

Chapter Eleven: Measuring Impact.point: 假设测试成功不等于达成结果，必须继续衡量对期望结果的影响
Chapter Eleven: Measuring Impact.core: However, an outcome-focused product trio needs to stay focused on the end goal—driving the desired outcome. We need to remember to measure not just what we need to evaluate our assumption tests, but also what we need to measure impact on our outcome.
Chapter Eleven: Measuring Impact.case: In our traditional “What type of job do you want?” interface, only 36% of students started a search. Two thirds of our site visitors never even started their job search. With our new “Tell us what you studied” interface, 83% of our visitors started their search.
Chapter Eleven: Measuring Impact.explain: 新界面让搜索启动率从36%升至83%，但这只是假设测试的先行指标；团队仍需追踪它是否真正带动期望结果，而非止步于中间指标上涨。

Chapter Twelve: Managing the Cycles.point: 测试后决定不做也是成果，发现工作的价值常在于省下的时间
Chapter Twelve: Managing the Cycles.core: The fruit of discovery work is often the time we save when we decide not to build something.
Chapter Twelve: Managing the Cycles.case: This was a big surprise for Mina’s team. Even though they had heard late payments come up as a pain point in interview after interview and they had market research reinforcing what they had heard, the results of their assumption tests were clear. Their customers did not want Simply Business to help them with this problem.
Chapter Twelve: Managing the Cycles.explain: Mina团队通过假设测试发现，尽管访谈和市场调研都指向逾期付款痛点，客户却并不想要Simply Business提供这项帮助，及时放弃避免了无效开发。

Chapter Thirteen: Show Your Work.point: 直接抛结论会引发意见之争，应展示推导过程
Chapter Thirteen: Show Your Work.core: When we present our conclusions, we aren’t sharing the journey we took to reach those conclusions. Instead, we are inviting our stakeholders to an opinion battle—a battle we have no chance of winning.
Chapter Thirteen: Show Your Work.case: However, when they shared their progress with the rest of the company, they ran into a significant roadblock. The sales team pushed back. They didn’t want to sell something new. They wanted to give their prospects what they were asking for—a journey builder just like what the competition offered.
Chapter Thirteen: Show Your Work.explain: Airship团队若只抛出结论，销售团队只会争论喜不喜欢；他们改为展示发现与推导，让销售参与其中，讨论才转向为什么是这个方案。

Chapter Fourteen: Start Small, and Itera.point: 不等许可，从自己能控制的小事开始接近客户
Chapter Fourteen: Start Small, and Itera.core: Instead of asking for permission or waiting for someone to show you how, start small. Iterate from there.
Chapter Fourteen: Start Small, and Itera.case: I asked to attend their conferences. I spent time talking to the journal editors. I read the discussion forums in our product to learn more about end-users’ research. I mined our feedback channels, looking for needs and pain points. I built feedback loops directly into the product. I didn’t know how to get direct access to our end-users, so I looked for every proxy I could find.
Chapter Fourteen: Start Small, and Itera.explain: 作者没有等待组织授权或现成方法，而是主动参加客户会议、访谈编辑、读论坛与反馈渠道，用一切可及的替代渠道接近终端用户，正是从小处起步、逐步迭代的体现。
